Cyberdreigingen zijn geen IT-probleem al: Cyber threats are not an IT-only problem; they affect strategy, cash flows, processes, people and risk insurance. This guide helps business owners step-by-step to translate external signals (news, national exercise outcomes, sector alerts) into concrete decisions, assigned owners and verifiable outcomes. A relevant example: the NCSA reports that the Netherlands participated in the European cyber exercise Cyber Europe 2021 and that government-wide cyber exercises took place in 2020 — this illustrates that threats and exercise experience are followed up structurally at the national level (source: open.overheid.nl/…/pdf). Use such external signals as a starting point, not an end goal.
1) Signaal: waar je op moet letten (exte: 1) Signal: what to watch for (external + internal) - External signals: warnings from NCSC/NCSA, sector- or supply-chain alerts, reported incidents at suppliers, legislative changes or exercise reports (e.g., Cyber Europe). - Internal signals: increase in unhandled security alerts, longer response times, failing backups, rise in helpdesk tickets after phishing campaigns.
2) Context & gevolg: vertaal het signaal: 2) Context & consequence: translate the signal into business impact - Do a quick impact mapping: which process, which customer group and which revenue stream does the signal affect? For example: a wave of ransomware among suppliers can halt production and block invoicing. - Specify consequences per domain: strategy (delay in product launch), objectives (missing monthly revenue target), money (liquidity risk due to outage), processes (production stoppage), people (increased workload), risks (compliance fines, reputational damage).
3) Beslissing: kies één prioriteit en wi: 3) Decision: choose one priority and appoint an owner For every high- or medium-high-impact signal determine: - Decision: what do we decide now? (example: 'We will run a tabletop exercise within 4 weeks focused on supplier disruption') - Owner: who is responsible? (example: IT manager executes, CEO facilitates, CFO assesses budget impact) - Measurement point: how do we know the decision is effective? (example: play time in exercise, percentage of restored services within SLA)
4) Actie: concreet stappenplan (gesloten: 4) Action: concrete step-by-step plan (closed improvement loop) Follow this 7-step loop for each signal with impact: 1. Collect signal: log external alert and internal anomaly reports (owner: security analyst). 2. Outline context: complete a one-page impact mapping (owner: process owner). 3. Estimate consequence: prioritize by urgency and business value (owner: management team/CEO). 4. Make decision: choose one priority, set budget and timeline (owner: CEO/CFO). 5. Deploy action: conduct tabletop/exercise, patching, additional monitoring or contract revision (owner: IT/security/operations). 6. Measure result: measure detection time, response time, recovery time and percentage of critical systems recovered (owner: IT + Business Control). 7. Learn and recalibrate: update playbooks, SLAs and training; record lessons learned (owner: continuous improvement lead).
5) Meetpunten en voorbeelden van control: 5) Metrics and examples of verifiable outcomes Choose 2–4 metrics per action. Examples: - Time to detect (MTTD): establish target and baseline; measurable for each incident/exercise. - Time to restore (MTTR) for critical processes: % of simulations within the target horizon. - Phishing response: % of employees who open a simulation link; goal is a decrease after training. - Recoverability: % of critical assets with a recent successful recovery test. - Financial check: estimated revenue impact based on hours of downtime per incident.
6) Mensen, processen en geld: praktische: 6) People, processes and money: practical allocation - People: name role owners (CEO: decision & culture, CFO: budget & insurance, IT/Security: execution, HR: training & awareness, Operations: process recovery). - Processes: update incident response playbook, change management and supplier contracts. - Money: treat exercise costs and remediation measures as investments in risk reduction; ask the CFO to create a simple business case: exercise costs vs. scenario costs of 1 day of downtime.
7) Risicobeheer & compliance Gebruik ext: 7) Risk management & compliance Use external reports and exercise findings (such as the mentioned national/European exercises) to strengthen your compliance and insurance position. Document decisions and tests — that helps with accountability to regulators and insurers.
